Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep casual tone, contractions, emoji, and the original request. Return correct text unchanged.", "input": "Mara: I’m setting up a desktop shortcut for the little map viewer on my Linux laptop. Ivo: On my Fedora machine, Super+M is free in the keyboard settings, but check your desktop environment before assigning it. GNOME and KDE don’t always show the same defaults, even when the key names look familiar.

Mara: Good point. I’m on Ubuntu with GNOME, and I don’t want to replace the overview key or change what M does inside other apps. This should only launch Fieldglass from the desktop.

Nadia: I use a similar shortcut for a timer. In Settings, open Keyboard, then View and Customize Shortcuts; the custom shortcuts section is near the bottom. Mine lists both the command and the key combination.

Mara: I found the custom shortcuts panel. It asks for a name, a command, and a shortcut. The package is installed from a Flatpak remote, so I’m checking the launch command before I save anything.

Theo: For Flatpak, `flatpak run org.example.Fieldglass` should work if that’s the app ID. You can confirm the exact ID with `flatpak list`; the display name alone might not be the command.

Mara: The list shows `org.river.Fieldglass`, so I’ll use that instead. I haven’t assigned the keys yet, and I’m glad I checked; the example ID would not have launched my copy.

Ivo: Right, use `flatpak run org.river.Fieldglass`. If you want to test it first, paste the command into a terminal. It should open the app without needing a special working directory.

Mara: It opens from the terminal. I’m going to add the shortcut now and leave the name as “Fieldglass map.” The label is just for the settings list, right?

Nadia: Yep, the name is only there to help you recognize it later. I have entries called “Kitchen timer” and “Screenshot folder,” and neither label changes what the command does.

Mara: Saved it as Super+M. The settings panel accepted the combination, but I’m not closing my unsaved notes yet; first I want to see whether the app opens from another workspace too.

Theo: That’s a useful check. Try it from a regular window and then from an empty workspace. Some desktop actions are tied to the active session, but a custom launch command should be available in either place.

Mara: It opens in both places, and the existing overview still comes up when I use Super by itself. I also tested M in the text editor, where it still types the letter normally.

Ivo: Nice. One thing to watch: if the shortcut ever stops responding after an update, check whether GNOME still has Super+M assigned to another action. Don’t reinstall the app before checking that.

Mara: I checked the built-in list before saving, and there wasn’t another Super+M entry. I’ll keep that note with the setup instructions, since I forget where custom shortcuts live between machines.

Nadia: I keep a small text file in my home folder with the app ID and command, but not the key binding. The key binding is desktop-specific, so I record it separately for each computer.

Mara: That makes sense. My laptop and desktop both run Linux, but the desktop is KDE, so I won’t assume the GNOME steps apply there. I’ll check its own shortcut settings later.

Theo: In KDE, look under System Settings and then Shortcuts; the wording can vary a little by release. You can add an application command there, but don’t copy the GNOME menu path into your notes as if it were universal.

Mara: I added a note that says “Ubuntu laptop: GNOME keyboard settings; desktop: check KDE shortcuts.” I’m leaving the desktop unconfigured for now because I haven’t decided which key combination feels comfortable there.

Ivo: Sensible. Also, if you use an external keyboard, make sure the Super key is recognized the way you expect. Some compact boards label it differently, and a key remapping utility can change its behavior.

Mara: The laptop keyboard has the usual Super logo, and the combination registers consistently. I tried it with Fieldglass closed and already running; in both cases, the shortcut brings the map viewer forward.

Nadia: That matches what I see with my timer. If the application is already open, the desktop may focus its existing window rather than start a second copy. It’s worth checking what the app itself does.

Mara: Fieldglass brings the current window forward, which is what I wanted. It doesn’t create a duplicate map window, and I don’t need a separate command-line option for the location I’m viewing.

Theo: You could put a location argument in the command if Fieldglass supports one, but I wouldn’t add it unless you actually want the shortcut to open the same place every time. The plain launch command keeps it flexible.

Mara: Agreed. I’ll keep the command plain for now. My maps change depending on the field visit, so a fixed location would be more annoying than useful.

Ivo: For anyone following along, the short version is: verify the Flatpak app ID, test the launch command, then bind an unused combination in the desktop’s own settings. Don’t assume another Linux desktop uses the same menu path.

Mara: I added those steps to my notes, along with the exact app ID. I’m not sharing the whole file here because it also has unrelated device details, but the shortcut entry itself is only a name and command.

Nadia: I label my notes with the computer name and desktop environment. That has saved me from trying to reproduce a GNOME shortcut on the KDE machine in the lab, where the settings page is in a different place.

Mara: I’ve named this note “Ubuntu laptop shortcuts” and dated it today. If I change the key combination later, I’ll update the entry rather than keep two conflicting versions in the same file.

Theo: One last practical detail: a custom shortcut may be stored in your desktop profile, not in the Flatpak package. Reinstalling Fieldglass shouldn’t be the first troubleshooting step if the key stops working.

Mara: Got it. The app command is still useful from the terminal, and the shortcut is configured separately in GNOME. I’ll check each part on its own if something changes after an update.

Ivo: Sounds like a clean setup. I’m going to try the same process with a notes app, but I’ll pick a different combination so it doesn’t collide with the map viewer when I’m working beside you.

Mara: Perfect. I’ll keep Super+M for Fieldglass on this laptop, and we can compare notes about KDE after I’ve had a chance to use the desktop for a few days.", "output": "Mara: I’m setting up a desktop shortcut for the little map viewer on my Linux laptop.
